title: Iimbotyi
author: Mama Nolwazi
desc: Speckled sugar beans soaked overnight and boiled soft in stock, then finished in a pan with softened onion and garlic — plain, patient, and one of the seven colours on a Sunday plate.
longDesc: Sometimes the beans are the dish. Iimbotyi is sugar beans done properly: an overnight soak, an hour and a half at a rolling boil, and then a brief second act in a pan with onion and garlic that lifts them out of being merely boiled. They turn up beside pap, beside rice, and as one of the components on a seven colours plate, where their job is to be the brown among the beetroot and the pumpkin.
ingredients: 360 g (2 cups) speckled sugar beans, soaked overnight
950 ml (4 cups) chicken or vegetable stock
240 ml (1 cup) water, to top up if needed
steps: Drain the soaked beans and put them in a saucepan with the stock and a little salt.
Bring to a rolling boil and cook for 1 1/2 hours, stirring occasionally, until the beans are soft all the way through.
Top up with the cup of water if the liquid gets low — beans that cook dry will catch and split.
Drain the beans and set them aside.
Heat the oil in a frying pan and fry the onion gently until softened, then add the garlic and fry for 3 minutes more.
Add the beans, stir them through the onion and garlic, check the seasoning and serve.
chefTips: Do not salt the soaking water, and go lightly on the salt in the boil. Heavily salted water toughens bean skins.
A rolling boil rather than a simmer is what the recipe calls for, and it works — but it drinks liquid, so keep the kettle nearby.
Use vegetable stock to keep it plant-based. The version with chicken stock is the commoner one but the beans do not need it.
They are better made a day ahead. The skins relax and the beans take up more of the onion.
commonMistakes: Skipping the overnight soak, which adds an hour to the cooking and still gives unevenly done beans.
Letting the pot boil dry, so the beans split and the bottom layer scorches.
Salting hard at the start, which leaves the skins tough.
Frying the onion until brown. It should be soft and sweet, not caramelised — there is nothing else here to balance a bitter edge.
storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days. Freezes for 3 months.
reheating: Reheat gently in a pan with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Sugar beans are high in plant protein, fibre, folate and iron.
Low glycaemic index, so they release energy slowly.
Naturally low in fat before the oil goes in.
culturalNote: Beans are the protein that does not need refrigeration, which is why every South African culinary strand has a version of them — iimbotyi in isiXhosa, ubhonsisi in isiZulu, dinawa in Setswana, and boontjiebredie in Afrikaans. The bag of dried beans in the cupboard is the most democratic ingredient in the country.
